text: A children's summer of dares and spying on the house next door, and then a courtroom those children were never meant to enter. Maycomb, Alabama arrives at the height of a six-year-old; Scout gets the town's business in fragments, and Mulligan holds to her scale even after the material stops being childish. Her father is a widower who reads in the evenings, and also the lawyer who agreed to defend Tom Robinson against a manufactured charge. Both of those men live in the same house for 129 minutes. The Academy's citations went to the black-and-white cinematography, the art direction, and the lead performance, which is to say to the town and the man standing in it. The trial is the engine; the subject is the week a child works out that the adults around her are choosing, not simply behaving.

A younger couple accepts a drink after midnight from the senior professor and his wife, and then cannot find the moment to leave. Nichols shoots the evening as a siege of one living room: the hosts are having an argument they have plainly been having for years, but now there is an audience, and an audience changes what an argument is for. The cruelty is rehearsed. What the guests supply is occasion, since a wound counts double when it is inflicted in front of witnesses, and the younger pair spend the night learning how much of their own marriage is available for the same treatment. From a cast of four, both leads drew Academy citations. 131 minutes, one house, and the drinks keep coming; the fascination is in two people who know exactly where the other one is thin.

A man arrives in Helsinki, is beaten nearly to death, and wakes with no name to give anyone. What follows is a comedy, though nobody in it raises a voice. Stripped of a biography, he has to acquire in sequence the things a person usually inherits, a place to sleep and work and someone to eat with, and Kaurismäki treats each acquisition as a full event: a moody dog attaches itself to him, a Salvation Army volunteer becomes the reason to want anything at all. The frames stay still and the faces stay nearly blank, which is exactly where the jokes live. Ninety-seven minutes; Cannes gave it the Grand Prix. The romance proceeds at the pace of two people who have decided there is no hurry, which is also the pace at which a life gets rebuilt.

An actor nobody will hire invents a woman who can be hired, and the daytime serial that casts her has no idea. The comedy is professional before it is romantic: Michael Dorsey cannot get work as himself, and Dorothy Michaels is the only version of him anyone will pay. Pollack builds the farce out of working hours, a shooting schedule, a costume that has to survive a full day, a lie with a call time attached, so the pressure stays administrative rather than moral. Then comes the complication that actually costs: as Dorothy he is liked, and consulted, and the people extending that trust are people he wants something from. The 1982 picture sits in the National Film Registry. Its real subject is not the disguise but the bill the disguise runs up with everyone who believes it.

Melvin Dummar said a will made him an heir to Howard Hughes, and the film built from that claim is far more interested in Melvin. Demme takes the hard-luck life at face value, the jobs and the payments due and the run of small American luck that never quite lands, and lets the Hughes fortune hover above it like weather. Ninety-five minutes, drawn from real events, and nobody on screen is granted the dignity of knowing whether the story is true. The original screenplay was honored by the Academy and the Writers Guild, and the National Society of Film Critics named it the best picture of its year. What is at risk here is not money. It is the chance that a man's one extraordinary encounter becomes the only thing anyone ever asks him about.

The funeral is over before the weekend starts; what remains is a house, seven old friends, and two days with nothing scheduled in them. Kasdan lets the group do the work, kitchens and hallways and one conversation splitting into two, somebody always half-listening from the next room, and gives none of them a task. The weekend has no agenda, which turns out to be the least forgiving structure available. With no plot to hide behind, seven people have to account for the distance between who they were together at twenty and the jobs, marriages and settlements they arrived in, and the only one exempt from explaining himself is the man they came to bury. It runs 105 minutes, holds a People's Choice Award and a place in the National Film Registry, and trades in small talk that keeps failing to stay small.

Rome, 1957: a woman is robbed by the man she trusts, left in the water, pulled out, and then she goes back to work. Recurrence is Cabiria's whole method. She absorbs the humiliation, fixes her face, and walks out again the next evening with her hopes intact and slightly rearranged. Fellini shoots her small and quick-tempered, defiant in a way that plays as comic until it stops playing; the film is filed as both drama and comedy, which is accurate, since the same scene is often both. It carries the Academy's international feature honor and a place on 100 film italiani da salvare, the Italian register of works to be preserved. None of that explains the hold it has. Her hopefulness is not innocence: she has the evidence, keeps it, and bets against it anyway.

A kidnapper and his hostage spend enough hours together to turn courteous, and then one of them asks the other for a favor. The premise is a hostage thriller; the texture is an unexpected bond between two men who should not have one. Keeping that promise means leaving Ireland, an IRA cell and a plan behind, and going to London to find a woman Fergus knows only from someone else's description. Jordan runs two clocks: the political one, which does not forgive a man who walks off, and the private one, in which a stranger becomes a habit. The machinery is real enough, with Jude and Maguire hunting him, but the film keeps stopping to let people talk. Recognized by the Academy for direction and editing, and placed on the BFI's hundred British films, it is finally about a man being decent at the least convenient moment of his life.

A man who cleans the sewers under Paris has stopped praying, and the film spends its length carrying him up toward the light. Borzage made it in 1927 and set it in the city of the 1910s, and the vertical arrangement is also the plot: work below the pavement, a life to be climbed toward, and a street waif with nowhere else to be. The Academy cited its lead actress and its director in a category called Best Director (Dramatic Picture), a name that dates the ceremony precisely. Borzage risks sentiment with no irony in it, two poor people improvising a household, filmed as though their belief in each other were load-bearing rather than a mood. The peril is the register: one wrong degree and it collapses. 119 minutes of that, and it never once blinks.

The hiring of a gardener is the only event in the house, and it is enough to restart something that had settled. James Whale made Frankenstein, Bride of Frankenstein and The Invisible Man; by 1957 he is retired, half-hidden, and keeping company mostly with images from his own past. Condon puts three people in that house, the director, the housekeeper who disapproves of nearly everything about him, and the young man cutting the grass, and lets what each one misreads in the others carry the picture. The adapted screenplay drew the Academy's citation, and the film holds the Independent Spirit for best feature and the National Board of Review's best film. The gardener is handsome and literal. Whale is neither. Their friendship runs on mutual misunderstanding, which is the joke until it is the other thing, across 105 minutes in which the monsters appear only as the memory of the man who made them.

Making a drinking companion the Archbishop of Canterbury is a way of buying the Church, and it works only as long as he stays a drinking companion. Henry II's calculation is sound, and the film watches it come apart at conversational speed: 148 minutes, largely two men in rooms, a friendship renegotiated as a constitutional problem. The Academy cited the lead performance, and the color art direction and cinematography that surround it. The pageantry is real, and the Golden Globe for best dramatic picture came with it, but the drama is small and verbal, closer to a divorce than a war. What Becket forfeits by accepting the office is the one relationship in which he was allowed to be casual. What Henry loses is harder for him to name, which is why he keeps talking.

Eighty-five minutes long, with a train due at noon: the running time and the deadline are nearly the same object. Zinnemann builds his Western out of errands rather than gunplay, as Will Kane goes door to door through a small New Mexico town putting a reasonable question to people who have reasons of their own. Each conversation costs him minutes he cannot spare, and the editing, which the Academy cited, is what makes the arithmetic felt. The genre usually supplies a community worth defending; this one asks what a sheriff is actually owed, and by whom. The film has been kept in the National Film Registry, and its lead performance carries an Academy citation too. Everything rides on a decision Kane makes early and then has to keep making again all morning.

Alice Sycamore is the only person in her household who could pass for ordinary, and she has fallen for the son of a banker who disapproves of everything her family is. Capra sets two economies against each other in 1938 and gives the better jokes to the side with less money: a house where everyone manufactures something nobody requested, against a fortune that depends on nobody being embarrassing. The dinner is the machine. One evening, everybody in the wrong room, and 126 minutes of preparation so the collision reads as a judgment on a way of living rather than a gag. Academy citations followed for Capra's direction and for the picture itself. The evening decides whether Alice's people are a choice or an accident, and she is the only one who has ever had to wonder.

Five hundred euros is the whole of the drama, that being what a hospital wants in advance before it will operate. Senada is thirty-one, five months pregnant, uninsured, bleeding, and sent home. Tanović films the arithmetic that follows at the length it deserves, seventy-five minutes, with a family whose income is scrap metal, weighed and sold. There is no villain in the room, only a rule applied by people who did not write it, and the precision of the film is in counting how few unreasonable steps it takes to reach a household with no options and a clock running. Berlin gave it the Grand Jury Prize and an acting Silver Bear, and it went forward as an international submission to the Academy. The stakes are stated in the first minutes and never rise; they only get nearer.
